a: Ramathaim-zophim
p: The Hebrew "Zophim" may be a copying slip for "a Zuphite." The Greek reads the name differently.

readings.en: from Ramathaim-zophim
readings.plain: Ramathaim-zophim

readings.en: from Armathaim Sipha
readings.plain: Armathaim

readings.en: from Ramathaim, a Zuphite
readings.plain: Ramathaim. He was a Zuphite

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the received name. The emendation is attractive but is a guess; it changes nothing important, since 1:1 names Zuph as an ancestor anyway.
b: "Zophim" ends in m, and the next Hebrew word begins with m, so many scholars think the m was written twice and the original was "a Zuphite," matching the ancestor Zuph later in the verse. The town is called simply Ramah everywhere else (1:19; 2:11).

a: a single portion worth two
t: A double portion or a single one?
p: The Hebrew phrase is obscure. The Greek says Elkanah gave Hannah one portion because she had no child.

readings.en: one portion of two faces (?)
readings.plain: a single portion worth two

readings.orig: μερίδα μίαν, ὅτι οὐκ ἦν αὐτῇ παιδίον
readings.en: one portion, because she had no child
readings.plain: a single portion, because she had no child

why: The Greek may be guessing at a hard word. The Hebrew, read with the ancient Jewish tradition (Targum: "a choice portion"), gives a better sense with "because he loved Hannah."
b: Appayim usually means "nostrils" or "face," and also "anger." Rashi and the Targum took the phrase to mean a choice or double share. The Greek reading, "one portion, since she had no child," would mean Hannah got only her own share, though Elkanah loved her. Some scholars think the Greek reflects a different Hebrew ('efes ki, "only") and prefer it.

a: Hannah got up.
p: The Greek adds that Hannah "stood before the LORD."

readings.en: and Hannah arose
readings.plain: Hannah got up.

readings.orig: καὶ ἀνέστη Αννα ... καὶ κατέστη ἐνώπιον κυρίου
readings.en: and Hannah arose ... and stood before the Lord
readings.plain: Hannah got up and stood before the LORD.

why: The Greek words look like an explanation of where Hannah went; the shorter Hebrew is kept.
b: The Greek places the words after "after they had eaten" and makes clear that Hannah went to pray at the sanctuary. Some scholars, including McCarter, think the words are original and were lost from the Hebrew. The meaning is the same either way: 1:10 shows her praying before the LORD.

a: No razor will ever go up on his head.
p: The Greek adds that the child will drink no wine or strong drink, making him a full Nazirite. The scroll probably had the same words.

readings.en: and a razor will not go up on his head
readings.plain: No razor will ever go up on his head.

readings.w: Septuagint (Codex Vaticanus); probably 4QSam-a (by the space in the scroll)
readings.orig: καὶ οἶνον καὶ μέθυσμα οὐ πίεται, καὶ σίδηρος οὐκ ἀναβήσεται ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and wine and strong drink he will not drink, and iron will not go up on his head
readings.plain: He will drink no wine or strong drink, and no razor will ever go up on his head.

why: The Greek words fill out the Nazirite vow from Numbers 6:3 and Judges 13:4. The scroll is broken here, and its support is inferred only from the space the line needs, so the evidence is weaker than at 1:22–24. The Hebrew is kept.
b: The Hebrew mentions only the razor, as with Samson (Judges 13:5). The Greek adds the rule about wine from the Nazirite law (Numbers 6:3). Earlier in the verse the Greek also has Hannah promise to give the child "as a gift (doton) until the day of his death." Both texts point to Samuel as a lifelong Nazirite. Compare 1:22, where the Dead Sea scroll names him a Nazirite outright.

a: Eli said to her,
p: In the Greek, it is Eli's servant who rebukes Hannah, not Eli himself.

readings.en: and Eli said to her
readings.plain: Eli said to her,

readings.orig: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ τὸ παιδάριον Ηλι
readings.en: and Eli's servant said to her
readings.plain: Eli's servant said to her,

why: In 1:15–17 Hannah answers "my lord" and Eli speaks to her, so the story flows best with Eli; the Greek may soften Eli's blunder.
b: The Greek spares the old priest the embarrassment of mistaking prayer for drunkenness. The Hebrew keeps Eli's mistake, which fits the book's portrait of a man who cannot see well, in body or in judgment (3:2; 4:15).

a: The woman went off, and she ate,
p: The Greek says Hannah went to her room and ate and drank with her husband.

readings.en: and the woman went on her way and ate
readings.plain: The woman went off, and she ate,

readings.orig: καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἡ γυνὴ εἰς τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτῆς καὶ εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ κατάλυμα αὐτῆς καὶ ἔφαγεν μετὰ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς καὶ ἔπιεν
readings.en: and the woman went on her way, and went into her lodging, and ate with her husband, and drank
readings.plain: The woman went off to her lodging and ate and drank with her husband,

why: The Greek adds detail that ties back to 1:7–9; the shorter Hebrew is kept.
b: The Greek makes the reunion of Hannah and Elkanah explicit. Either way, Hannah's eating marks the end of her fast and grief (1:7). Some see the Greek as an expansion; a few think the Hebrew lost the words.

a: stay there for good
p: The Dead Sea scroll adds: "and I will give him as a Nazirite forever, all the days of his life."

readings.en: and he will stay there forever
readings.plain: stay there for good

readings.orig: ונתתיהו נזיר עד עולם כול ימי חייו
readings.en: and I will give him as a Nazirite forever, all the days of his life
readings.plain: stay there for good. I will give him as a Nazirite for all time, all the days of his life

why: The scroll's words repeat the vow of 1:11 and 1:28. They may be original, but they could also be an early scribe making Samuel's Nazirite status explicit, so the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and reports the scroll here.
b: This is the clearest place where 4QSam-a names Samuel a Nazirite. The Mishnah ends Nazir with the debate whether Samuel was one (Mishnah Nazir 9:5). The scroll's reading shows that some Jews before the time of Jesus read Samuel that way. The Greek here follows the Hebrew more closely. Whether the words are original or a pious explanation is debated.

a: Only may the LORD bring about what you have spoken.
t: Whose word: the LORD's or Hannah's?
p: The Hebrew says "may the LORD establish his word." The Dead Sea scroll and the Greek say "what has come out of your mouth."

readings.en: what goes out from your mouth
readings.plain: Only may the LORD bring about what you have spoken.

readings.en: only may the LORD establish his word
readings.plain: Only may the LORD make his word come true.

why: No word of the LORD has been spoken to Hannah in the story; Hannah has spoken the vow. The scroll and the Greek fit the context, and the Hebrew is easily explained as a scribe's change to a familiar phrase.
b: The Masoretic reading has puzzled readers, since no word of the LORD has been given about the boy. Rashi and others answered that the "word" is Eli's blessing in 1:17. The scroll, older than the Masoretic Text by a thousand years, and the Greek read "what came out of your mouth," Hannah's own vow, which Elkanah now confirms (compare Numbers 30:10–15).

a: a bull three years old
t: Three bulls or a three-year-old bull?
p: The Hebrew has "three bulls"; the Dead Sea scroll and Greek read "a three-year-old bull." Only one bull is killed in 1:25.

readings.en: with a bull three years old
readings.plain: a bull three years old

readings.en: with three bulls
readings.plain: three bulls

why: 1:25 speaks of "the bull," one animal. The Hebrew letters for "three-year-old bull" and "three bulls" differ only by the division of words, so a copying slip is easy to see.
b: Hebrew bprm shlshh ("bulls, three") and bpr mshlsh ("a bull, three-year-old") use nearly the same letters. A three-year-old animal was mature and valuable (Genesis 15:9). The scroll, the Greek and the Syriac all have the single bull, and nearly all modern translations follow them. The scroll and the Greek also add "and bread" to the offerings.

a: The boy was just a little boy.
p: The Hebrew's strange phrase "and the boy was a boy" is replaced in the Greek by a longer account of the sacrifice.

readings.en: and the boy was a boy
readings.plain: The boy was just a little boy.

readings.orig: καὶ τὸ παιδάριον μετ᾽ αὐτῶν. καὶ προσήγαγον ἐνώπιον κυρίου, καὶ ἔσφαξεν ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ τὴν θυσίαν
readings.en: and the child was with them. And they came before the Lord, and his father slaughtered the sacrifice
readings.plain: The boy was with them. They came before the LORD, and his father slaughtered the sacrifice.

why: The Hebrew is hard but makes sense as "the boy was young"; the Greek looks like a smoothing that also explains whose sacrifice it was.
b: The Greek and 4QSam-a have a longer text here and in 1:25. Scholars such as McCarter think the Hebrew lost a line by a scribe's skip; others think the Greek filled in. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and reads its odd phrase as stressing how young Samuel was.

a: And he bowed down there before the LORD.
p: The Hebrew says "he bowed down"; some Hebrew copies say "they." The Greek leaves the words out; the scroll seems to read "she."

readings.en: and he bowed down there to the LORD
readings.plain: And he bowed down there before the LORD.

readings.en: and they bowed down
readings.plain: And they bowed down there before the LORD.

readings.en: (no words)
and she left him there and bowed down
readings.plain: She left him there and bowed down before the LORD.

why: The witnesses disagree, and the scroll is broken here. The received text is kept; "he" may be Elkanah or the boy himself.
b: The verse is a puzzle of who is acting. Elkanah has hardly been mentioned since 1:23, and the boy is very young. The scroll, as its editors restore it, places Hannah at the center, which fits the story; but the letters are damaged. The Greek has a similar line at 2:11 instead (see there).

a: and he weighs what people do
p: The written Hebrew says deeds are "not" weighed; the reading tradition says they are weighed "by him."

readings.en: and by him deeds are weighed
readings.plain: and he weighs what people do

readings.en: and deeds are not weighed
readings.plain: and are not deeds measured?

why: The spoken reading fits the line about God's knowledge and is supported by the Targum. The written form can only work as a question.
b: Lo "to him" and lo' "not" sound alike, and Hebrew scribes mixed them often. This is one of the places where the Masoretes noted that the text should be read one way though written another (see 2:16). The Greek reads "God prepares his own designs."

a: He keeps the feet of his loyal ones safe,
t: A different line in the Greek
p: The Greek begins this verse with "granting the vow to the one who vows, and he blessed the years of the righteous."

readings.en: he guards the feet of his faithful ones
readings.plain: He keeps the feet of his loyal ones safe,

readings.orig: διδοὺς εὐχὴν τῷ εὐχομένῳ καὶ εὐλόγησεν ἔτη δικαίου
readings.en: granting the prayer to the one who prays, and he blessed the years of the righteous
readings.plain: He grants the vow of the one who vows, / and blesses the years of the righteous.

why: The Greek line fits Hannah's own story, her vow and its answer, which is why some think it is a later adaptation; the Hebrew line fits the poem's contrast of the faithful and the wicked.
b: Parts of the Greek line appear also in 4QSam-a, which shows that a Hebrew text like it existed. The song in the Greek is shaped more closely to Hannah's situation. The Greek also lacks some of the following Hebrew. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: As for the LORD, those who quarrel with him are smashed;
p: The Greek adds a passage like Jeremiah 9:23–24: let the wise and the strong not boast, but boast in knowing the LORD.

readings.en: the LORD, his adversaries are shattered
readings.plain: As for the LORD, those who quarrel with him are smashed;

readings.orig: κύριος ἀσθενῆ ποιήσει ἀντίδικον αὐτοῦ, κύριος ἅγιος. μὴ καυχάσθω ὁ φρόνιμος ἐν τῇ φρονήσει αὐτοῦ ...
readings.en: the Lord will make his adversary weak; the Lord is holy. Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom ...
readings.plain: The LORD makes his opponent weak; the LORD is holy. Let the wise not boast of their wisdom, nor the strong of their strength, nor the rich of their riches; but let the one who boasts boast in this: in understanding and knowing the LORD, and in doing justice and right in the land.

why: The Greek addition matches Jeremiah 9:23–24 closely and looks like a reader's echo added to a song about pride and humility. The Hebrew is kept.
b: The song's theme, the LORD humbling the proud, invited the addition. 4QSam-a may also have had a longer text here, but it is broken. The Greek addition is an early witness to how Hannah's song was read alongside the prophets. Paul quotes the Jeremiah saying in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

a: Elkanah went off to his house in Ramah.
p: The Greek reads "They left him there before the LORD and went away to Armathaim."

readings.en: and Elkanah went to Ramah, to his house
readings.plain: Elkanah went off to his house in Ramah.

readings.orig: καὶ κατέλιπον αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ ἐνώπιον κυρίου καὶ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Αρμαθαιμ
readings.en: and they left him there before the Lord and went away to Armathaim
readings.plain: They left him there before the LORD and went away to Ramah.

why: The Hebrew brings Elkanah back after the song, which is natural if the song was set into an older story; the Greek is smoother but looks like a way of closing the scene after it.
b: The leaving of Samuel is placed differently in each witness. At 1:28 the scroll 4QSam-a, as its editors restore it, reads "she left him there and bowed down," while the Masoretic Text has "he bowed down" and the Greek has nothing. Here at 2:11 the Greek has "they left him there," the parents together, where the Hebrew names Elkanah. The differences show how the song of 2:1–10 was fitted into the story in more than one way.

a: No! You will give it now.
p: The written Hebrew has "to him"; the reading tradition and ancient versions have "No!"

readings.w: Masoretic Text, as read (qere); Septuagint, Targum
readings.en: No! For now you will give it
readings.plain: No! You will give it now.

readings.en: to him: For now you will give it
readings.plain: he would say to him, "You will give it now."

why: The spoken reading gives the sharper sense and is supported by the ancient versions. The same pair of sound-alike words appears in 2:3.
b: The Masoretes marked many places where lo, "to him," and lo', "not," were confused. Either way, the priest's servant demands the meat raw, before the fat has been offered to God.

a: May the LORD repay you with children from this woman, in return for the one lent to the LORD.
p: The Hebrew says "may the LORD give you seed"; the Dead Sea scroll says "repay you," and the Greek agrees. Who lent the boy also differs.

readings.orig: ישלם יהוה לך זרע ... השאלה אשר השאילה ליהוה
readings.en: may the LORD repay you seed from this woman in exchange for the loan which she lent to the LORD
readings.plain: May the LORD repay you with children from this woman, in return for the one lent to the LORD.

readings.orig: יָשֵׂם יְהוָה לְךָ זֶרַע מִן־הָאִשָּׁה הַזֹּאת תַּחַת הַשְּׁאֵלָה אֲשֶׁר שָׁאַל לַיהוָה
readings.en: may the LORD give you seed from this woman in exchange for the request which he asked of the LORD
readings.plain: May the LORD give you children from this woman, in place of the one asked of the LORD.

why: "Repay" fits the idea of exchange in "in return for," and "she lent" matches Hannah's own words in 1:28. The Hebrew "he asked" makes Elkanah the actor, which does not fit 1:20–28.
b: This verse plays on sha'al, "ask" and "lend," the root behind Samuel's story (1:20; 1:27–28) and also Saul's name. The scroll and the Greek make Hannah the one who lent the boy, as she says in 1:28. Repayment comes in 2:21: three sons and two daughters.

a: Eli had grown very old.
p: The Dead Sea scroll adds Eli's age here: ninety-eight, the age the Hebrew gives at 4:15.

readings.en: and Eli was very old
readings.plain: Eli had grown very old.

readings.orig: ועלי זקן מאד בן תשעים ושמנה שנה
readings.en: and Eli was very old, ninety-eight years old
readings.plain: Eli had grown very old, ninety-eight years old.

why: The age is given in its natural place at 4:15, just before Eli's death, and the scroll's plus looks like a reader bringing it forward. The Plain English Translation keeps the shorter line here.
b: The plus matters for 4:15: it shows that a Hebrew text a thousand years older than the Masoretic Text also had ninety-eight, against the Greek's ninety. The same verse in the scroll lacks the clause about the women at the tent of meeting (see the next entry).

a: He kept hearing of all the things his sons did to all Israel.
p: The Hebrew adds that Eli's sons lay with the women who served at the tent of meeting. 4QSam-a and the main Greek text lack it.

readings.en: (the sentence ends here)
readings.plain: He kept hearing of all the things his sons did to all Israel.

readings.orig: וְאֵת אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכְּבוּן אֶת־הַנָּשִׁים הַצֹּבְאוֹת פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד
readings.en: and that they lay with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting
readings.plain: He kept hearing of all the things his sons did to all Israel, and that they lay with the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

why: The Plain English Translation follows the shorter text, on the same grounds as at 2:20 and 2:33. Two independent witnesses lack the clause. Its wording is taken from Exodus 38:8, and it calls the sanctuary the "tent of meeting," while these chapters call Shiloh's sanctuary a "temple" with doors and a doorpost (1:9; 3:15). Those are signs of a later addition, not of an accidental loss.
b: Exodus 38:8 speaks of the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting, with the same rare verb tsava', used of organized service; their role is unknown. Most text critics, including McCarter and Tov, regard the clause here as added from Exodus. If so, the charge against Eli's sons in the oldest text concerns the sacrifices only. The Talmud took the clause as an overstatement: Rabbi Jonathan said the sons only delayed the women's offerings (Bavli Shabbat 55b). Most English versions keep the clause.

a: slaves in Pharaoh's household
p: The scroll and the Greek read "slaves to Pharaoh's house." The Hebrew has "belonging to Pharaoh's house."

readings.en: slaves to the house of Pharaoh
readings.plain: slaves in Pharaoh's household

readings.en: to the house of Pharaoh
readings.plain: belonging to Pharaoh's household

why: Two independent witnesses agree, and the short Hebrew phrase is awkward without a noun. A word was easily lost before "to the house."
b: The point of the line is the exodus: God revealed himself to Levi's family when they were slaves, and freed them to be priests. The NRSV and ESV also follow the longer reading.

a: kick at my sacrifice and my grain offering
p: The Hebrew says Eli's house "kicks at" God's sacrifices. The Greek says they look on them "with a greedy eye."

readings.en: why do you kick at my sacrifice and my offering
readings.plain: kick at my sacrifice and my grain offering

readings.orig: ἵνα τί ἐπέβλεψας ἐπὶ τὸ θυμίαμά μου καὶ εἰς τὴν θυσίαν μου ἀναιδεῖ ὀφθαλμῷ
readings.en: why have you looked on my incense and my sacrifice with a shameless eye
readings.plain: look with greedy eyes on my incense and my sacrifice

why: The Hebrew is rare but has a parallel in Deuteronomy 32:15, "Jeshurun grew fat and kicked," which fits "fatten yourselves" later in this verse.
b: The Greek may reflect a different Hebrew verb (tabbit, "look") and a phrase about a greedy eye. The Hebrew words that follow, "which I commanded for my dwelling," are also hard, and the Plain English Translation renders them as "the ones I ordered for my home."

a: I will chop off your arm and the arm of your ancestor's family
p: The Hebrew says God will cut off Eli's "arm," his strength. The Greek reads "your seed," his descendants.

readings.en: and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house
readings.plain: I will chop off your arm and the arm of your ancestor's family

readings.orig: καὶ ἐξολεθρεύσω τὸ σπέρμα σου καὶ τὸ σπέρμα οἴκου πατρός σου
readings.en: and I will destroy your seed and the seed of your father's house
readings.plain: I will wipe out your descendants and the descendants of your ancestor's family

why: The Hebrew "arm" (zeroa') and "seed" (zera') are written with nearly the same letters. "Arm" fits the verb "chop off" (gada'), used of cutting down horns and trees, and is the harder image; the Greek may have read the easier word.
b: Either way, the threat is to Eli's line: no one in his house will grow old. The arm stands for strength, as in "the arm of the LORD" (Isaiah 53:1).

a: No one in your house will live to be old.
p: 4QSam-a lacks this line. It goes with the variant at 2:32, where the same idea is repeated.

readings.en: so that there will be no old man in your house
readings.plain: No one in your house will live to be old.

readings.en: (no words)

why: The Greek supports the Hebrew here, and the scroll's shorter text at this point stands alone. The Plain English Translation keeps the line; at 2:32, where the scroll and the Greek agree, it follows the shorter text.
b: 2:31b and 2:32b say almost the same thing, which is a sign that the Hebrew combines two forms of the oracle. Each witness keeps one or both. See the note and variant on 2:32.

a: There will not be an old man in your house for all time.
p: 4QSam-a and the main Greek text lack the first half of the Hebrew verse. It goes with the variant at 2:31.

readings.en: (the verse begins here)
readings.plain: There will not be an old man in your house for all time.

readings.orig: וְהִבַּטְתָּ צַר מָעוֹן בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר־יֵיטִיב אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל
readings.en: and you will look at distress in the dwelling, in all that he does good for Israel
readings.plain: In my dwelling you will see trouble, while good things are done for Israel. There will not be an old man in your house for all time.

why: Two independent witnesses lack the words, which are hard to construe and repeat the thought of 2:31. The Plain English Translation follows the shorter text, as at 2:20, 2:22 and 2:33.
b: The lost words are among the most obscure in the chapter (see the note). Many scholars, including McCarter, think they arose as a variant form of 2:31b that was later copied into the text alongside it.

a: All the rest of your family will fall to men's swords.
t: "Die as men" or "fall by the sword"?
p: The Hebrew says the rest "will die as men," and speaks of "your" eyes. The scroll and Greek read "his" eyes and "fall by the sword of men."

readings.en: they will fall by the sword of men
readings.plain: All the rest of your family will fall to men's swords.

readings.en: and all the increase of your house will die as men
readings.plain: All the rest of your family will die as grown men.

why: The Hebrew "die as men" is hard to make sense of, and the scroll gives a clear, older reading that the massacre at Nob in 22:18–19 fulfills. The scroll and the Greek also read "his eyes" in the first line, which the Plain English Translation follows.
b: The Masoretic "your eyes ... your soul" makes Eli himself the grieving one, though he will be dead. The scroll and the Greek read "his eyes ... his soul," the survivor's grief, which most take as Abiathar, who escapes Saul's massacre (22:20) and is later banished by Solomon (1 Kings 2:26–27). The Talmud took "die as men" as dying young, in their prime (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18a).

a: His sons were cursing God
p: The Hebrew says the sons "cursed themselves" (or "for themselves"); the Greek says "they spoke evil of God."

readings.en: because his sons were speaking evil of God
readings.plain: His sons were cursing God

readings.en: because his sons were cursing for themselves
readings.plain: His sons were bringing a curse on themselves

why: Jewish tradition itself lists this verse among the "corrections of the scribes" (tiqqune soferim), places where scribes changed a word to avoid writing that someone cursed God. The Greek preserves the older reading.
b: Hebrew lahem, "for themselves," differs from elohim, "God," by only two letters. Ancient lists of the scribal corrections, preserved in the Masorah, include this verse. Cursing God was a capital crime (Leviticus 24:15), which explains both the scribes' discomfort and the severity of the judgment.

a: At Shiloh the LORD made himself known to Samuel by the word of the LORD.
p: The Greek adds that Samuel was trusted as a prophet everywhere, and that Eli was very old while his sons went on in their evil way.

readings.orig: כִּי־נִגְלָה יְהוָה אֶל־שְׁמוּאֵל בְּשִׁלוֹ בִּדְבַר יְהוָה
readings.en: for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD
readings.plain: At Shiloh the LORD made himself known to Samuel by the word of the LORD.

readings.orig: ... καὶ ἐπιστεύθη Σαμουηλ προφήτης γενέσθαι τῷ κυρίῳ εἰς πάντα Ισραηλ ἀπ᾽ ἄκρων τῆς γῆς καὶ ἕως ἄκρων. καὶ Ηλι πρεσβύτης σφόδρα, καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ πορευόμενοι ἐπορεύοντο καὶ πονηρὰ ἡ ὁδὸς αὐτῶν ἐνώπιον κυρίου
readings.en: ... and Samuel was trusted to be a prophet of the Lord to all Israel from one end of the land to the other. And Eli was very old, and his sons kept on going, and their way was evil before the Lord
readings.plain: At Shiloh the LORD made himself known to Samuel by the word of the LORD. Samuel was trusted as the LORD's prophet in all Israel, from one end of the land to the other. Eli was very old, and his sons went on in their ways, and their way was evil before the LORD.

why: The Greek lines repeat 3:20 and 2:22 and look like a bridge written to lead into the war of chapter 4. The Hebrew is kept.
b: The Greek has a second plus at 4:1 that makes the Philistines start the war (see there). Together the two pluses give the Greek a smoother join between Samuel's call and the ark story. Some scholars think the Hebrew lost them; most see them as expansions.

a: Israel marched out to meet the Philistines in battle
p: The Greek adds: "And in those days the Philistines gathered for war against Israel."

readings.en: and Israel went out to meet the Philistines for battle
readings.plain: Israel marched out to meet the Philistines in battle

readings.orig: καὶ ἐγενήθη ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις καὶ συναθροίζονται ἀλλόφυλοι εἰς πόλεμον ἐπὶ Ισραηλ· καὶ ἐξῆλθεν Ισραηλ
readings.en: and it happened in those days that the Philistines gathered for war against Israel; and Israel went out
readings.plain: In those days the Philistines gathered for war against Israel, and Israel marched out to meet them in battle

why: The Greek may preserve a line lost from the Hebrew, but the shorter text makes sense and is kept.
b: The Greek makes the Philistines the attackers and Israel the defenders. The Hebrew leaves Israel's reason unstated, which some readers take as Israel going to war without asking God, a point that fits the disaster that follows. McCarter thinks the Greek line is original.

a: sitting on his seat beside the road
t: Beside the road or beside the gate?
p: The Hebrew is hard to read here. The Greek says Eli sat "beside the gate, watching the road."

readings.en: on the seat beside the road, watching
readings.plain: sitting on his seat beside the road

readings.en: (an unclear word) road
readings.plain: sitting on his seat by (?) the road

readings.orig: ἐπὶ τοῦ δίφρου παρὰ τὴν πύλην σκοπεύων τὴν ὁδόν
readings.en: on the seat beside the gate, watching the road
readings.plain: sitting on his seat beside the gate, watching the road

why: The read form gives good sense. The Greek agrees with 4:18, where Eli falls "beside the gate," and may be harmonizing.
b: The written Hebrew yakh is not a known word; the reading tradition corrects it to yad, "side." The Greek's "gate" fits 4:18. The Plain English Translation keeps "beside the road" here and "beside the gate" in 4:18, as in the Hebrew.

a: Eli was ninety-eight.
p: The Hebrew gives Eli's age as ninety-eight; the main Greek text says ninety. The Dead Sea scroll supports ninety-eight.

readings.en: ninety-eight years old
readings.plain: Eli was ninety-eight.

readings.en: and Eli was ninety years old
readings.plain: Eli was ninety.

why: Ninety-eight has two independent witnesses: the Masoretic Text here and 4QSam-a at 2:22. The Greek round number looks like a simplification.
b: Rahlfs's text, following Codex Vaticanus, has "ninety." The scroll gives the age earlier, at 2:22 (see there), but with the same number as the Hebrew. Eli's great age explains his blindness and his fatal fall (4:18).

a: For forty years he had judged Israel.
p: The Hebrew says Eli judged Israel forty years; the Greek says twenty.

readings.en: and he judged Israel forty years
readings.plain: For forty years he had judged Israel.

readings.orig: καὶ αὐτὸς ἔκρινεν τὸν Ισραηλ εἴκοσι ἔτη
readings.en: and he judged Israel twenty years
readings.plain: For twenty years he had judged Israel.

why: Forty is the round number for a generation used for several judges (Judges 3:11; 5:31; 8:28). The Greek may preserve a different count, but there is no strong reason to prefer it.
b: The Greek's twenty matches Samson (Judges 15:20) and the twenty years of 7:2. Some scholars think forty was brought in to match the round numbers of Judges. Either way, the note places Eli among the judges and closes his era.

a: Only the main part of Dagon was left.
p: The Hebrew says "only Dagon was left on him." The Greek says "only the back of Dagon was left."

readings.en: only Dagon was left on him
readings.plain: Only the main part of Dagon was left.

readings.en: only the back of Dagon was left
readings.plain: Only the back of Dagon was left.

why: The Hebrew likely means "only Dagon's trunk"; many scholars think a word like "his body" (gevo) dropped out. The Plain English Translation gives the sense without adding a guessed word.
b: The Greek "back" or "spine" may reflect a Hebrew word that has been lost. Rabbinic and medieval tradition (Radak) took "Dagon" here as the fish-shaped lower part, from dag, "fish"; that idea is now doubted, since Dagon was a grain god (see 5:2).

a: He ruined them and struck them with swellings, in Ashdod and all around it.
p: The Greek adds that mice swarmed in the land and there was great panic in the city. Mice appear in the Hebrew only in chapter 6.

readings.en: and he devastated them and struck them with swellings
readings.plain: He ruined them and struck them with swellings, in Ashdod and all around it.

readings.orig: ... καὶ μέσον τῆς χώρας αὐτῆς ἀνεφύησαν μύες, καὶ ἐγένετο σύγχυσις θανάτου μεγάλη ἐν τῇ πόλει
readings.en: ... and in the middle of its land mice sprang up, and there was a great confusion of death in the city
readings.plain: He ruined them and struck them with swellings, in Ashdod and all around it. Mice sprang up in the middle of their land, and there was a great panic of death in the city.

why: The Greek line prepares for the gold mice of 6:4–5, which the Hebrew introduces without warning. That could mean the Hebrew lost it, or that the Greek filled the gap; the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew.
b: Many scholars, including McCarter, think the Greek reflects an original reference to mice. If so, the plague may have been carried by rodents, a link people in the ancient world may have noticed. The Greek repeats the mice in 6:1. Compare the note on the swellings.

a: you will find out why his hand would not leave you alone
p: The Hebrew says "it will be known to you" why God's hand stayed on them. The Greek says "atonement will be made for you."

readings.orig: וְנוֹדַע לָכֶם לָמָּה לֹא־תָסוּר יָדוֹ מִכֶּם
readings.en: and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn from you
readings.plain: you will find out why his hand would not leave you alone

readings.orig: καὶ ἐξιλασθήσεται ὑμῖν· μὴ οὐκ ἀποστῇ ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν
readings.en: and atonement will be made for you; will not his hand then turn from you?
readings.plain: atonement will be made for you. Then surely his hand will leave you alone

why: The Hebrew makes good sense: the test of 6:9 is how the Philistines will find out. The Greek reading fits the guilt offering, but may come from it.
b: The Greek reflects Hebrew vekhuppar lakhem, "and it will be atoned for you," which differs from venoda' lakhem by a few letters. 4QSam-a is reported to agree with the Greek, but the scroll is broken here, and this entry does not rely on it. The NRSV follows the Greek.

a: as far as the big stone
p: The Hebrew has "Abel the great." The Greek and Targum read "the great stone," which fits 6:14–15.

readings.en: as far as the great stone
readings.plain: as far as the big stone

readings.en: and as far as Abel the great
readings.plain: as far as Great Abel

why: Hebrew even, "stone," and avel, "meadow" or "mourning," differ by one letter that was easily confused. The great stone has just been named in 6:14–15.
b: Jewish readers kept the Hebrew "Abel" and linked it to the mourning in 6:19 (Rashi). The Targum, though, already reads "stone." Most modern translations follow the Greek and Targum.

a: But he struck at the men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the LORD's ark.
p: The Greek reads: "The sons of Jeconiah did not rejoice among the men of Beth-shemesh when they saw the LORD's ark."

readings.orig: וַיַּךְ בְּאַנְשֵׁי בֵית־שֶׁמֶשׁ כִּי רָאוּ בַּאֲרוֹן יְהוָה
readings.en: and he struck among the men of Beth-shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD
readings.plain: But he struck at the men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the LORD's ark.

readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἠσμένισαν οἱ υἱοὶ Ιεχονιου ἐν τοῖς ἀνδράσιν Βαιθσαμυς, ὅτι εἶδαν κιβωτὸν κυρίου
readings.en: and the sons of Jeconiah did not rejoice among the men of Beth-shemesh, because they saw the ark of the Lord
readings.plain: But the family of Jeconiah did not join the rejoicing of the men of Beth-shemesh when they saw the LORD's ark.

why: The Greek gives a reason for the judgment (one family's failure to rejoice) and may well be original, but it is hard to judge how it arose. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and reports the Greek here.
b: Many scholars, such as McCarter, prefer the Greek, since the Hebrew "looked into" is an unusual phrase. The Greek makes the guilty party a single family, priests perhaps, who did not honor the ark's return. Either way, the ark's holiness is the theme (6:20).

a: seventy men
t: Seventy or fifty thousand and seventy?
p: The Hebrew says "seventy men, fifty thousand men." Josephus and a few Hebrew manuscripts have only seventy.

readings.w: Josephus, Antiquities 6.16; a few medieval Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: seventy men
readings.plain: seventy men

readings.en: seventy men, fifty thousand men
readings.plain: seventy men, fifty thousand men

why: The Hebrew has no "and" between the numbers and puts them in an odd order. Beth-shemesh was a small town. The extra "fifty thousand" looks like an addition, perhaps a note in the margin.
b: The Talmud already puzzled over the number and explained that the seventy were each worth fifty thousand (Bavli Sotah 35b). Josephus, who knew a text close to 4QSam-a, has only seventy. Most modern translations read seventy, some with a footnote.

a: between Mizpah and Shen
p: "Shen" means "tooth" and is not otherwise known. The Greek and Syriac read "Jeshanah," a town near Bethel.

readings.en: and between Shen
readings.plain: between Mizpah and Shen

readings.en: and between the Old (Jeshanah)
readings.plain: between Mizpah and Jeshanah

why: The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew name, since "Shen" may be a crag ("tooth" of rock) whose name has not survived. The Greek reading is plausible, but a guess at an unknown place.
b: The Greek translator read yeshanah, "old," which is a town on Judah's border with Ephraim (2 Chronicles 13:19). Many modern translations follow it. Either way, the stone marks the line where the Philistine advance was stopped.

a: the best of your cattle
p: The Hebrew says the king will take "your best young men"; the Greek reads "your best cattle," which fits the list of animals.

readings.orig: καὶ τὰ βουκόλια ὑμῶν τὰ ἀγαθά
readings.en: and your good herds
readings.plain: the best of your cattle

readings.en: and your good young men
readings.plain: your best young men

why: The verse lists slaves and donkeys; cattle fits between them. The young men were already taken in 8:11–12. Hebrew bqrkm ("your cattle") and bchwrykm ("your young men") look alike.
b: Most modern translations follow the Greek. The pair "cattle and donkeys" is a common Hebrew pair (Exodus 22:4), and the speech moves from people to property.

a: for I have seen my people
t: Seen my people, or their affliction?
p: The Greek reads "I have looked on the affliction of my people," as in Exodus 3:7.

readings.en: for I have seen my people
readings.plain: for I have seen my people

readings.orig: ὅτι ἐπέβλεψα ἐπὶ τὴν ταπείνωσιν τοῦ λαοῦ μου
readings.en: for I have looked on the affliction of my people
readings.plain: for I have seen the suffering of my people

why: The Greek may preserve a word lost from the Hebrew, but it also matches the familiar line of Exodus 3:7, which a scribe could easily bring in. The shorter Hebrew is kept.
b: The RSV and NRSV follow the Greek. Either way, God's words echo the call of Moses, and Saul is sent as a rescuer like Moses (see the note).

a: A bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down.
t: Talking or sleeping on the roof?
p: The Hebrew says Samuel "spoke with Saul on the roof." The Greek says "they spread a bed for Saul on the roof, and he lay down."

readings.orig: καὶ διέστρωσαν τῷ Σαουλ ἐπὶ τῷ δώματι, καὶ ἐκοιμήθη
readings.en: and they spread a bed for Saul on the roof, and he lay down
readings.plain: A bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down.

readings.en: and he spoke with Saul on the roof
readings.plain: He spoke with Saul on the roof.

why: The next verse begins "They got up early," and Samuel calls to Saul "on the roof," so Saul had slept there. The Hebrew letters for "he spoke" and "they spread" are close, so a copying error is likely.
b: Hebrew vaydabber ("and he spoke") and vayyirbedu ("and they spread") share most letters. The Hebrew reading, a private talk on the roof, appealed to readers who imagined Samuel explaining kingship to Saul, but the story only shows Samuel's message the next morning (9:27).

a: as ruler over his people Israel? You will rule the LORD's people and rescue them from the power of the enemies around them. And this will be your sign that the LORD has anointed you ruler over his inheritance:
t: A sentence lost by a skip
p: The Greek and Latin have a longer text. The Hebrew probably lost it when a scribe's eye jumped between two places that read "the LORD has anointed you."

readings.orig: εἰς ἄρχοντα ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ Ισραηλ; καὶ σὺ ἄρξεις ἐν λαῷ κυρίου, καὶ σὺ σώσεις αὐτὸν ἐκ χειρὸς ἐχθρῶν αὐτοῦ κυκλόθεν. καὶ τοῦτό σοι τὸ σημεῖον ὅτι ἔχρισέν σε κύριος ἐπὶ κληρονομίαν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἄρχοντα
readings.en: as ruler over his people, over Israel? And you will rule among the people of the Lord, and you will save them from the hand of their enemies around. And this is the sign to you that the Lord anointed you ruler over his inheritance
readings.plain: as ruler over his people Israel? You will rule the LORD's people and rescue them from the power of the enemies around them. And this will be your sign that the LORD has anointed you ruler over his inheritance:

readings.en: has not the LORD anointed you ruler over his inheritance?
readings.plain: as ruler over his inheritance?

why: The longer text explains why Samuel goes on to list signs (10:2–7). The phrase "the LORD has anointed you" occurs twice in it, a classic place for a scribe's eye to skip. Its words echo 9:16, and the rare verb "rule" ('atsar) of 9:17 appears again in it.
b: This is one of the clearest cases of the Hebrew losing text by a skip (homoioteleuton). Most modern translations include the longer text. Without it, the Hebrew jumps from a question to a list of signs with no mention of what the signs prove.

a: who is their father?
p: The Hebrew says "their father"; the Greek, Syriac and Latin say "his father," pointing to Kish.

readings.en: and who is their father?
readings.plain: who is their father?

readings.en: and who is his father?
readings.plain: who is his father?

why: The harder reading is the Hebrew, and it can be explained (see the note). "His father" looks like an attempt to make the question refer to Saul's family, which Saul's name has already supplied.
b: If "his father," the question asks scornfully about Saul's family, or about the parentage of whoever prophesies. If "their father," the question is about the prophets, perhaps their leader. See the note on this verse for the readings.

a: Then Saul son of Kish was picked.
p: The Greek adds that the family of the Matrites was brought forward man by man before Saul was picked.

readings.en: and Saul son of Kish was taken
readings.plain: Then Saul son of Kish was picked.

readings.orig: καὶ προσάγουσιν τὴν φυλὴν Ματταρι εἰς ἄνδρας, καὶ κατακληροῦται Σαουλ υἱὸς Κις
readings.en: and they bring forward the clan of Mattari man by man, and Saul son of Kish is taken
readings.plain: They brought the family of the Matrites forward man by man, and Saul son of Kish was picked.

why: The Greek fills in the step from family to man that the pattern of Joshua 7:17–18 expects. It may preserve lost words, but the Hebrew makes sense.
b: The Hebrew jumps from the family straight to Saul, which some scholars think is a scribe's skip. The Greek also lacks the household step. Either way, the lot works down to one man, who then cannot be found.

a: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had been harshly oppressing the Gadites and the Reubenites. He put out every right eye they had, and no one rescued Israel. Among the Israelites across the Jordan, not a man was left whose right eye Nahash king of the Ammonites had not put out. But seven thousand men had escaped from the Ammonites and had come to Jabesh-gilead.
p: A paragraph about Nahash, missing from the Hebrew and Greek, survives in 4QSam-a and in Josephus. It goes with the change at the start of 11:1.

readings.orig: ונ[ח]ש מלך בני עמון הוא לחץ את בני גד ואת בני ראובן בחזקה ונקר להם כ[ו]ל עין ימין ...
readings.en: And Nahash king of the Ammonites oppressed the Gadites and the Reubenites harshly, and gouged out every right eye of theirs ...
readings.plain: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, had been harshly oppressing the Gadites and the Reubenites. He put out every right eye they had, and no one rescued Israel. Among the Israelites across the Jordan, not a man was left whose right eye Nahash king of the Ammonites had not put out. But seven thousand men had escaped from the Ammonites and had come to Jabesh-gilead.

readings.en: (no paragraph); the Hebrew ends the verse "But he kept silent"

why: The paragraph is in the oldest manuscript of Samuel, and Josephus's Bible had it. It explains why Nahash demands right eyes and why seven thousand Israelites were in Jabesh, and no clear motive for adding it has been shown. Its loss is generally taken as a scribe's accident, though the exact trigger is debated (Cross; Tov). The Plain English Translation includes it. Part of one clause is damaged: Cross restored "and he gave Israel no rescuer," others "and he put terror and dread on Israel"; the Plain English Translation's "no one rescued Israel" follows Cross.
b: Frank Moore Cross published the paragraph in 1980 and argued it is original, and McCarter and Ulrich agree. The NRSV (1989) was the first major English translation to print it; the NIV and ESV mention it in a footnote. Others, such as Alexander Rofé and David Tsumura, think it is a learned expansion that explains the story, written in the style of Judges. The scroll itself shows a scribe skipping and then correcting between the lines in this passage, a reminder of how easily lines were lost. In the scroll, the paragraph is followed by 11:1 beginning "About a month later" (see there).

a: About a month later,
t: "He kept silent" or "about a month later"
p: The Hebrew ends 10:27 "But he kept silent." The scroll and Greek read "about a month later," which begins 11:1. It goes with the Nahash paragraph in 10:27.

readings.en: and it was about a month
readings.plain: About a month later,

readings.en: and he was like one keeping silent (end of 10:27)

why: The Hebrew letters of "like one keeping silent" (kmchrysh) and "like a month" (kmchdsh) differ by one letter, r for d, which look almost the same in Hebrew. The scroll and Greek give the time phrase that leads into the next story, and Josephus agrees.
b: In the Masoretic Text Saul's silence answers the sneers of 10:27, and many traditional readers admire it. With the Nahash paragraph restored, "about a month later" connects the refugees of 10:27 with the siege of Jabesh. The Plain English Translation follows the scroll; readers of the Hebrew will find Saul's silence at the end of 10:27.

a: three hundred thousand Israelites and thirty thousand men of Judah
p: The Greek has six hundred thousand of Israel and seventy thousand of Judah. The Dead Sea scroll also has seventy thousand for Judah.

readings.en: three hundred thousand ... thirty thousand
readings.plain: three hundred thousand Israelites and thirty thousand men of Judah

readings.en: six hundred thousand ... seventy thousand
readings.plain: six hundred thousand Israelites and seventy thousand men of Judah

readings.w: 4QSam-a (Dead Sea Scroll, Cave 4) (the number for Israel is lost)
readings.en: seventy thousand (for Judah)
readings.plain: three hundred thousand Israelites and seventy thousand men of Judah

why: The case for Judah's seventy thousand is close: the scroll and the Greek agree, and Josephus has seventy thousand too. But the scroll's figure for Israel is lost, and the Greek's six hundred thousand echoes the exodus total (Exodus 12:37), so it looks like an increase. Rather than build a mixed count from a damaged scroll and an inflated Greek total, the Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic numbers and shows the others here.
b: Josephus gives seven hundred thousand for Israel and seventy thousand for Judah (Antiquities 6.78). Many scholars think elef, "thousand," first meant a military unit, which would make the real numbers far smaller (see the note at 4:2). The witnesses agree that the muster was huge and that Judah was counted separately.

a: they made Saul king
p: The Hebrew says "they made Saul king"; the Greek says "Samuel anointed Saul there as king."

readings.en: and they made Saul king there
readings.plain: they made Saul king

readings.orig: καὶ ἔχρισεν Σαμουηλ ἐκεῖ τὸν Σαουλ εἰς βασιλέα
readings.en: and Samuel anointed Saul there as king
readings.plain: Samuel anointed Saul as king

why: In the Hebrew the people act, which suits Samuel's word "renew" in 11:14; the Greek brings in Samuel and the anointing of 10:1, perhaps to tie the stories together.
b: David too was anointed privately by Samuel (16:13) and later made king by the people (2 Samuel 2:4; 5:3). The Hebrew reading fits that pattern. The Greek also makes Samuel, not Saul, lead the rejoicing at the end of the verse (see the next entry).

a: Saul and all the men of Israel
p: In the Hebrew, Saul and all Israel rejoice. In the Greek, it is Samuel and all Israel.

readings.en: Saul and all the men of Israel
readings.plain: Saul and all the men of Israel

readings.en: Samuel and all Israel
readings.plain: Samuel and all Israel

why: The next chapter shows Samuel far from rejoicing over the kingship (12:17). Saul's joy fits his day of victory. The Greek looks like a harmonizing with its own reading earlier in the verse.
b: The names Saul and Samuel are close in Hebrew (Sha'ul, Shemu'el) and easily confused. The difference matters: in the Hebrew, the day belongs to Saul.
